The laws with regard to bidi, sambddi, anubddi and bibadi cuide us
in the discernment and choice of those notes which are essentially important
in the formation of rdgas, and which immediately determine their true
nature; of those which should be admitted, and of those which should be

in short, are strictly observed in the melodic progression of a réga which
loses its agreeable effect when any of them is least infringed. We find
a parallel practice obtaining among the ancient Greeks under the name
of petteia,a part of melopwia, which taught them what sounds they
should reject, what they should admit, and what they ought to employ

most frequently. —

By bddé is meant that note which is always of the greatest utility
in the formation of a réga, and immediately ascertains its peculiar cha-
racter. Owing to its most frequent use and permanency, it predominates
over all the other notes that are admitted into a rdga, and plays the

most important part. It behoves us to remark here that in rdgabistdra,

Harmony, in its modern import, is not admissible, nor is it of much

harmony into our music, Captain Willard truly observes : “Indeed, so wide
is the difference between the natures of the European and Oriental music,

of that science.” Nevertheless, -Iindu music is not altogether void of
ikarmony Although harmony is not employed in our vocal performace,

Mirchchhané is distinct from gamaka with which it is generally con-
founded, the latter being a tremulous motion of voice, produced by the
rapid contraction and extension of the vocal chords. The gamaka is
nothing but the reiteration of the same note. It is one of the several
graces used in Hindu music, and plays an important part in the mani-

festation of a rdégu. Weshall now describe the manner of producing

misrchchhand in vocal as well as in instrumental performance. In the for-

mer, the vowel sound of the letter from which the mirchchhand com-
mences, is continued to the note to which it is intended to extend, in one
unbroken stream of voice ; while in the latter, the mirchchhand is produced
by the string relating to any fret being drawn out with pressure, either
by the forefinger, or by the middle finger, to express any of the succeed-

ing notes to which it should extend.

but also in the vikrita swaragréma or artificial scale. In all we have
